title: Pullback to the Moving Averages
teaches: The pullback to the moving averages as we trade it: a leader in a stacked, rising trend drifts quietly onto a rising 20 EMA or 50-day, a session closes at or above the line, the buy is a market order as price trades over that session's high, the stop sits a few cents under the pullback low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

walkthroughs.title: YELP, June 2013: the fast leader's quiet dip
steps: YELP, June 2013. A fast leader riding its rising short-term averages since February, then four quiet days back onto them.
Just 5.7% off the high, and volume dries up: the touch day trades on 0.60x volume.
June 26 it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 31.80. Stop a few cents under the low, 30.67.
A 3.6% stop is wider than we like, so fewer shares. If they give way, you're out. Instead, 3R next day.

walkthroughs.title: CAT, September 2025: the 50-day on a mega cap
steps: Mega caps do it too, just slower. CAT, September 2025: after a 4-month run, its first pullback to the rising 50-day.
Six days down on quiet volume, 5.7% off the high. A tight hold right on the line.
September 3 it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 418.13. Stop a few cents under the low, 410.47.
A 1.8% stop, right where we like it. If the line gives way, you're out. Instead, a two-week grind to 3R.

walkthroughs.title: MOH, June 2018: six quiet days on the line
steps: Watch the volume on this one. MOH, June 2018: six days sideways, 7.8% off the high, its rising short-term averages underneath.
Volume dries up to 0.4x, the lowest on the whole chart. Quiet like that raises the grade.
June 8 it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 86.93. Stop a few cents under the low, 85.82.
Only a 1.3% stop. If the line gives way, you're out small. It paid 3R in one session.

questions.q: A leader pulls back onto a moving average. What does that line need to be doing before you'll buy the dip?
choices: Rising, pointed up under price
Falling, so you buy the bounce
Flat, inside a range
Anything, a touch is a touch
questions.why: Rising. A rising line means the trend under the stock is still up, so the dip is just a rest inside it. Buyers have been stepping in higher and higher, and the line tracks that. Once it flattens or rolls over, that support is gone. Then you're just buying a stock that's going down. I check the slope before I ever look at the touch.
questions.lesson_line: Check the slope first. Only buy a dip onto a line that's still rising.

wrong.Falling, so you buy the bounce: A falling line is a downtrend. You'd be catching a stock that's still being sold.
wrong.Flat, inside a range: A flat line means the trend stalled. That's a warning, not support.
wrong.Anything, a touch is a touch: Buy every touch and you end up buying random lines. The slope comes first.

questions.simple: We want a rising line, because that means the trend under the stock is still up and the dip is just a rest.

reasons: the 10-session rising test is a proposed card number (map.line_rising)

questions.q: On pullbacks we like, price is over the 200-day and the 20 EMA sits over the 50 over the 200.
questions.why: True. That's what a leader looks like while it rests: everything stacked and pointed the right way. Price over the 200-day is the hard line, because we don't buy stocks under it. The 50 over the 200 is mostly a must, not always. The 20 over the 50 on top of that is what we like to see. It tells you the short, middle and long trends agree. A clean stack only puts the stock on your radar, though. You still need the dip, the hold and the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Price over the 200-day, averages stacked. That's a leader resting.
questions.simple: True. We want price over the 200-day and the averages stacked, the 20 over the 50 over the 200.

deeper.trap: Price over the 200-day is only half the picture. A stock can sit over the 200-day with its 20 EMA still under the 50. That's a stock repairing, not a leader resting.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, no longs below the 200-day) and the 200-day decision D-009 is held
the 50-over-200 order is the card's rule, not B26

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The stop sits a few ___ under the low, not exactly on it.
questions.why: Cents. The stop sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it. Stop first: the size comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the low.
questions.simple: A few cents. The stop sits just under the low, not exactly on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62, A3)
which low the stop sits under is held as D-008, so the question keys only 'a few cents'

questions.q: Tomorrow it trades over the hold day's high. How do you get in?
choices: Market order as it trades through
Limit order at the hold day's high
Buy the close if it holds up
Wait and buy the next morning
questions.answer: Market order as it trades through
questions.why: Market order, right as it trades through. The trigger is the hold day's high. When price takes it out, you're in. A limit at the high sounds tidy, but on a good day the stock runs straight through it and you're left unfilled. Buying the close or the next morning means paying up after the move started. This one reached 3R within two days. Set an alert at the high the night before, so you're ready.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger trades, you buy at market. The stop goes in right after.

wrong.Limit order at the hold day's high: On a strong trigger the stock runs through your limit and leaves you behind. We buy at market.
wrong.Buy the close if it holds up: We buy the trigger during the day, never the close. By the close the move can be gone.
wrong.Wait and buy the next morning: Waiting a day means buying higher, with the stop farther away, for nothing.

questions.simple: Buy at market the moment price trades over the hold day's high, during the session.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, market orders)
the buy trigger itself is held as D-003 and is not graded

questions.story: This is the day before. The pullback held its line, and the hold day just closed. Tomorrow price may trade over its high.

questions.q: A stock with an RS rating of 60 dips cleanly onto a rising line. It's strong enough for a pullback buy.
questions.why: False. We buy leaders, RS 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A 60 is a middle-of-the-pack stock. When it dips to a line, there's no real demand waiting there to catch it. We want leaders because they're the names big buyers keep adding to on dips. Check the RS rating before you look at anything else.
questions.lesson_line: Pullbacks are for leaders. RS 80 or more, or it's not our trade.
questions.simple: False. We want an RS rating of 80 or more, and 60 is a middle-of-the-pack stock.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)
when RS is read is held as D-011 and is never asked

questions.q: You like a pullback and you're ready to buy. How do you put the position on?
choices: Full size, one price, one stop
Half now, half on the next dip
A starter, then add if it works
Full size, lower the stop on dips
questions.answer: Full size, one price, one stop
questions.why: Full size, one price, one stop. That's how we buy everything. Your risk is set the moment you're in. One entry and one stop, and you know exactly what you lose if it fails. Scaling in or adding lower just means more shares in a trade that's going against you. And the stop only moves up, never down.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, full size. No starter, no scaling in.

wrong.Half now, half on the next dip: Buying the second half lower is averaging down. We buy the full size at one price.
wrong.A starter, then add if it works: We don't scale in. Full size goes in at once, with one stop.
wrong.Full size, lower the stop on dips: The stop only moves up. Lowering it just makes the loss bigger.

questions.simple: One buy at full size with one stop. We never add on a dip or lower the stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, adds settled as D-135)

questions.q: Look at the volume on those four days into the line. What's it telling you?
choices: Sellers are drying up
Buyers are losing interest
A breakdown is coming
Nothing, volume never matters
questions.why: Sellers are drying up. Four days of small bars on about half the normal volume. The people who wanted out are mostly gone, so volume dries up. Fewer shares are for sale, so when buyers come back, price can move. I like seeing it, and it raises the grade. It's not a must, though. A clean pullback without it can still be bought.
questions.lesson_line: When volume dries up into the line, the grade goes up.

wrong.Buyers are losing interest: On a dip into a rising line, light volume means few sellers. The selling is what's thin.
wrong.A breakdown is coming: A breakdown comes on heavy selling. Quiet volume into the line is the opposite.
wrong.Nothing, volume never matters: Volume isn't a must, but it's a tell. Volume drying up on the dip raises the grade.

questions.simple: Sellers are drying up. Quiet volume on the dip raises the grade, but it isn't a must.

reasons: +2 proposed card criterion (map.volume); the research scan found quiet volume made little difference

questions.story: The day before the trigger. A leader drifted four days down onto a rising moving average. The bars got small.

deeper.example: Minervini's template, as Deepvue writes it up, looks for the same thing: low volume during pullbacks.

questions.q: A low can poke a little under the line and still count as a touch, if the day closes back on it.
questions.why: True. A moving average isn't a wall, it's a zone. Stocks wick through it all the time, then close back on it. What I care about is the close. A small poke under that gets bought back the same day shows buyers defending the line. A low way under the line, or a close under it, is a different story.
questions.lesson_line: Treat the line as a zone. Judge it on the close.
questions.simple: True. The line is a zone, not one exact price, and a close back on it is what counts.

reasons: the touch range of 1 ATR under to 0.25 ATR over is a proposed card number (map.touch)

questions.q: A leader drifts toward its line. How do you judge whether the dip is a real rest or just noise?
choices: Against its own daily range
A fixed 1% off the high
Down 25% from the 52-week high
Any red day counts as a dip
questions.why: Against its own daily range. That's ATR, the average true range: how far the stock moves on a normal day. A fast leader can swing 1% before lunch on a quiet day. For that stock, 1% off the high is noise. For a slow stock it can be a real dip. So line the drift up against the stock's normal day, by eye on the chart. A fixed percent treats a slow stock and a fast leader the same, and they aren't.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the dip in the stock's own range, not a fixed percent.

wrong.Down 25% from the 52-week high: That's not a rest, that's a deep correction. Leaders pull back near their highs.
wrong.A fixed 1% off the high: A fixed percent treats every stock the same. A fast leader moves that much on a quiet morning.
wrong.Any red day counts as a dip: One red day is noise. A pullback is a few days of drift off the high.

questions.simple: Judge the dip against the stock's own normal daily range. A fixed percent treats every stock the same.

reasons: the 1 ATR minimum and the 11-session window are proposed card numbers (map.depth)

questions.q: How long should the drift into the line take on this setup?
choices: One session
A few days
Two to three weeks
A couple of months
questions.why: A few days. It's a short rest in a stock that's working: a few quiet days onto the line, then a hold. One sharp day down isn't a drift, it's a flush, and I'd want to see it settle first. Weeks of drift is a slower setup. On the 20 EMA, judge it as the 20 EMA pullback. Months sideways is a base, and then you're buying a breakout, not a pullback.
questions.lesson_line: A few quiet days onto the line. That's the rest we buy.

wrong.One session: One sharp drop isn't a rest. Let it settle and show you a hold first.
wrong.Two to three weeks: That's a slow drift. On the 20 EMA it belongs to the 20 EMA pullback.
wrong.A couple of months: Months sideways is a base. You'd buy the breakout, not a pullback.

questions.simple: A few days of quiet drift onto the line. One sharp drop is a flush, and months sideways is a base.

reasons: the 2 to 8 session length is a proposed card number (map.length)

questions.q: A pullback with one huge red bar, about three times a normal day's range, still counts as an orderly drift.
questions.why: False. Orderly means a quiet drift: small bars, no panic. One red bar three times a normal day's range is somebody dumping stock. It doesn't kill the setup on its own. But it's a warning, and it lowers the grade. I'd want to see the line hold on the close, and I'd be pickier about taking it.
questions.lesson_line: Orderly is small bars and no panic. One huge red bar breaks it.
questions.simple: False. One huge red bar is real selling, and it lowers the grade even if the setup is still alive.

reasons: the 2 ATR down-day limit is a proposed card number (map.orderly)

questions.q: The pullback has reached the line. What turns a session into the hold day?
choices: It closes at or above the line
It trades the most volume of the dip
It closes under the line
Its low never dips below the line
questions.answer: It closes at or above the line
questions.why: It closes at or above the line. The close is the vote at the end of the day. If buyers defended the line into the close, you have your hold. The low can poke under during the day, that's fine. Volume doesn't decide it. Once you have the hold, the trigger is the next trade over that day's high. The stop goes a few cents under the low.
questions.lesson_line: A close on the line is the hold. A trade over its high is the trigger.

wrong.It trades the most volume of the dip: Volume tells you how strong the day was. The close against the line names the hold.
wrong.It closes under the line: A close under the line isn't a hold yet. Wait for a close back on it.
wrong.Its low never dips below the line: The low can wick under. What counts is where it closes.

questions.simple: The hold day is the session that closes at or above the line. Then you wait for the trigger.

reasons: +2 ties to the held trigger decision D-003 (the buy follows the hold day)

questions.q: In an Orange market we take A+ setups only.
questions.why: True. The market reading sets the risk before the chart does. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange A+ only, Red mostly cash and shorts. Orange limits which setups we take. It is not a ban on trading.
questions.lesson_line: The market reading sets how much and which setups. Orange means A+ only.
questions.simple: In an Orange market we only take the best setups, the A+ ones, because the market reading sets the risk.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (F65)

questions.q: What's the lowest price and daily dollar volume we'll trade?
choices: $10 and $5 million a day
$20 and $100 million a day
No minimum if RS is 90
$10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 and $20 million a day. Under that, you can't get in and out clean. The spread eats you, and your stop can fill well below where you set it. A thin stock can look great on a chart and still be untradeable at real size. A high RS doesn't change that. I wouldn't even keep a thin name on the watchlist.
questions.lesson_line: $10 and up, $20 million a day and up. Thinner names don't get watched.

wrong.$20 and $100 million a day: That's stricter than we are. The floor is $10 and $20 million a day.
wrong.No minimum if RS is 90: Strong RS doesn't make a thin stock easy to sell. The floor still holds.
wrong.$10 and $5 million a day: The price floor is right, but $5 million a day is too thin. We want $20 million.

questions.simple: We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day, so we can get out clean.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (B23 price and volume floor)

questions.q: You're holding a pullback buy and it gaps down through your stop. Fill in what happens next.
questions.sentence: Gap through your stop? The first ___ minutes decide, and that bar's low is your new stop.
questions.why: 30. When a stock gaps through your stop, you can't get out at your price. It opened below it. So don't dump it on the first print. Let the first 30 minutes play out. The low of that first 30-minute bar is your new stop. If those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop.
questions.simple: Let the first 30 minutes decide. The low of that first 30-minute bar is your new stop.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (B20)
rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: You're in at 86.93 with the stop at 85.82. Where's 3R?
questions.why: 90.26. One R is your risk per share: 86.93 minus 85.82 is 1.11. Three of those is 3.33. Add that to 86.93 and you get 90.26. Mark it on the chart the day you buy. It's a yardstick for how the trade is going, not a sell order. This one got there the next session. We still very rarely sell on day 1 just because a number printed.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R the day you buy. It's a yardstick, not a sell order.
questions.simple: 3R is 90.26. It's a yardstick for the trade, not an order to sell.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, a third at 3R)
the buy trigger behind the example is held as D-003

wrong.$89.15: You added the three R to the stop instead of the buy.
wrong.$88.04: That's only one R up from the buy.
wrong.$91.37: That's four R, one too many.

questions.story: You bought as price traded over the hold day's high. The stop sits a few cents under the low.

questions.q: Is today the hold day?
choices: No, the low must stay above the line
No, it needs a second close above
Yes, it closed at or above the line
questions.answer: Yes, it closed at or above the line
questions.why: Yes. The touch day closed at or above the line, which makes it the hold day. Now wait for the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: One close at or above the line is the hold. The buy comes next, on the trigger.

wrong.No, the low must stay above the line: The low may touch or dip a little. The close is what counts.
wrong.No, it needs a second close above: One close at or above the line is the hold.

questions.story: A leader drifts four quiet days onto its rising 10-day. Today the low touched the line and it closed above it.

questions.q: You're in at 23.62 with the stop at 22.79. How wide is that stop, in percent?
questions.why: 3.5%. The gap is 23.62 minus 22.79, which is 0.83. Divide by your buy, 23.62, and you get 3.5%. Always divide by the buy, since that's what you paid. I prefer 1-3%, and 3.5% is still good. Up to 5% I'll take it. The size just comes down, so the dollars at risk stay the same.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop off your buy. 1-3% is ideal, up to 5% works.
questions.simple: The stop is 3.5% under the buy. That's still a good stop, so the size just comes down a bit.

deeper.trap: Divide the gap by the buy, not the stop. Dividing by the stop gives 3.6% and makes every stop look wider than it is.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, about 3%)

wrong.3.6%: You divided by the stop. Divide by the buy.
wrong.0.83%: That's the dollar gap, 0.83, not a percent.

questions.story: You bought as price traded over the hold day's high. The stop sits a few cents under the low.

questions.q: Minervini's trend template still passes a stock that sits 30% under its 52-week high.
questions.why: False. His template wants price within 25% of the 52-week high, and 30% under is outside it. The idea behind it is sound: leaders rest near their highs. A stock 30% off is repairing, not leading. We don't trade off his exact number, but I read every chart in percents. How far off the high comes first.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders rest near their highs. Deep under it is a repair job.
questions.simple: False. Minervini wants a stock within 25% of its high, and 30% under is outside it.

deeper.trap: Being near the high doesn't make it a buy. It just tells you the stock is acting like a leader. The rising line, the quiet dip and the hold still have to be there.

reasons: the 25% limit is a proposed card number (map.near_high), though Deepvue's Minervini page agrees

questions.q: Before the dip, what should the stock have done to make the pullback worth buying?
choices: A breakout, gap or new up-cycle
Sat for months under the 200-day
Fallen a month on heavy volume
Nothing, a rising line is enough
questions.answer: A breakout, gap or new up-cycle
questions.why: A breakout, an earnings gap or a new up-cycle. A pullback needs something to pull back from. When a stock just broke out or gapped on earnings, there's fresh demand behind it. The first dips after that are where buyers who missed it step in. A stock that's done nothing has nobody waiting on the dip.
questions.lesson_line: A pullback needs something to pull back from.

wrong.Sat for months under the 200-day: Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's no leader.
wrong.Fallen a month on heavy volume: A month of heavy selling is distribution, not a leader resting.
wrong.Nothing, a rising line is enough: A rising line alone isn't the story. Something has to have kicked off the run first.

questions.simple: A recent breakout, earnings gap or new up-cycle, because a pullback needs a run to pull back from.

reasons: +2 proposed card criterion (map.recent_catalyst), the Bonde line is one trader's list

deeper.example: Bonde lists the same idea as a common pullback method: buy the first pullback after a major breakout.

questions.q: It's at 3R the day after you bought. What do you do?
choices: Sell a third, 3R is the rule
Sell half and lock it in
Hold, it's early in the push
Sell it all before the close
questions.answer: Hold, it's early in the push
questions.why: Hold, it's early. This is only the second day. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. I very rarely sell on day 1, and most of the time I wait until day 3 at the earliest. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. Strength this early means the stock wants to go. This one reached 5R two sessions later.
questions.lesson_line: 3R early isn't a sell signal. Let the push work.

wrong.Sell it all before the close: Selling everything on a strong start is how you miss the big ones.
wrong.Sell a third, 3R is the rule: 3R isn't a sell signal. The first sell is a judgment, and this is early.
wrong.Sell half and lock it in: We very rarely sell this early. Let a strong push work.

questions.simple: Hold. The first sell is a judgment, and we very rarely sell this early in a push.

deeper.trap: 3R feels like a finish line. It's a yardstick. We often sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (B19: a third at 3R, breakeven 2R to 5R, default at the first trim)

questions.story: You bought as price traded over the hold day's high at 28.38, with the stop at 27.93. The next session it's already at 3R.

questions.q: On a steadier mover, you trail what's left under the 20 EMA and sell it on a close below.
questions.why: True. Fast movers ride the 9 EMA, steadier ones the 20 EMA. Pick the one the stock has respected on the way up. Then sell what's left on a close below it, not on a dip during the day. A steady stock wobbles under the 9 all the time. Trail it there and you'll get shaken out of a good trend.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 9 EMA. Steadier mover, 20 EMA. Sell on the close.
questions.simple: True. A steadier mover rides the 20 EMA, and we sell what's left on a close below it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (E52: the trail line depends on how fast the stock moves)

questions.q: Can you take the trigger tomorrow?
choices: Yes, the chart is too clean to skip
Yes, but at half size
No, earnings are too close
No, it needs a second close above
questions.why: No. We don't open a new buy in the 3 days before a report, and this one's in 2. An earnings gap can jump right over your stop. Then your planned loss turns into a much bigger one overnight. A clean chart doesn't change that, and half size doesn't either. Check the date before you check the chart. If it's still set up after the report, take it then.
questions.lesson_line: Check the earnings date before you check the chart.

wrong.Yes, the chart is too clean to skip: A great chart doesn't stop an earnings gap. No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Half size still gets gapped. The answer is no new buy inside the window.
wrong.No, it needs a second close above: One close on the line is the hold. Earnings is the reason to pass.

questions.story: The hold day just closed on a clean pullback. The company reports earnings in 2 sessions. Tomorrow it may trade over today's high.
questions.simple: No. We don't open a new buy in the 3 days before earnings, because a gap can jump the stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (B22 earnings window)

questions.q: The 52-week high is 300.00. On the hold day the stock closes at 238.00. How far off the high is it?
questions.why: 20.7%. The drop is 300.00 minus 238.00, which is 62. Divide by the high, 300.00, and you get 20.7%. I read every chart this way: how far off the high, how stretched over the averages. Leaders rest near their highs. 20.7% off is a real hole for a leader, so the rest of the chart has to be clean.
questions.lesson_line: Read the chart in percents. How far off the high comes first.
questions.simple: It's 20.7% off the high. Always divide the drop by the high, not the close.

reasons: +2 computed key (percent under the high)

wrong.26.1%: You divided by the close. Divide the drop by the high.
wrong.79.3%: That's where the close sits as a share of the high, not how far it fell.

deeper.example: Minervini's template draws its line at 25% under the 52-week high. We judge it by eye, but it's a useful yardstick.

questions.q: What's your move at 186?
choices: Nothing, my stop still decides
Buy more to lower the average
Move the stop under the new low
Sell half to cut the risk
questions.why: Nothing. You bought full size at 190 with one stop. The dip to 186 is just the stock being a stock. If the line holds, great. If it breaks, the stop takes you out at the loss you already planned. Adding here doubles down on a trade that isn't working yet. Lowering the stop makes the loss bigger. Sit on your hands.
questions.lesson_line: A dip after the buy changes nothing. Your stop still decides.

wrong.Buy more to lower the average: That's averaging down. We buy once, at one price.
wrong.Move the stop under the new low: The stop only moves up. Lowering it just grows the loss.
wrong.Sell half to cut the risk: Your stop already caps the loss. Selling half on a normal dip is fear, not a plan.

questions.story: You bought the hold on a rising 50-day at 190. Two days later it dips to 186 and holds the line again.
questions.simple: Nothing. One buy, one stop, and the stop you set still decides the trade.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (A4, A5, adds settled as D-135)

Yes, if volume stays quiet
No, the 50-day has rolled over
No, drifting means it's broken

questions.q: Your stock is ready, but the index just slipped. What decides whether you take the trigger?

Nothing, the stock is all that matters
Wait for the index to make a new high
Wait for the stock to make a new high
questions.answer: Our market reading and the grade

An index closing under its 20-day for the first time in weeks is worth noticing. It can be the start of a market pullback, or nothing. We had a clean NVDA pullback stopped out the same week the index started topping. If the reading still says go and this is a top setup, take the trigger. If the reading has slipped, get pickier and smaller.

wrong.Wait for the index to make a new high: That can take weeks. You'd sit out trades the market reading still lets you take.
wrong.Wait for the stock to make a new high: It already triggered. Waiting for a new high is just chasing it later.
wrong.Nothing, the stock is all that matters: Most stocks follow the market. Ignore it and good triggers fail more often.

questions.q: Does a three-day drop fit the length rule?
choices: Yes, 2 to 8 sessions covers it
No, it needs at least 5 sessions
No, a drop is never a pullback
Yes, the 50-day has no length rule
questions.why: Yes. The pullback lasts 2 to 8 sessions from the swing high to the touch day, and three days fits. The drop must also be orderly, with no single down day larger than 2 ATR. BFAM's dip was 2.24 ATR, past the 1 ATR minimum.
questions.lesson_line: Two to eight sessions, and three counts.

wrong.No, it needs at least 5 sessions: The rule is 2 to 8 sessions, so three fits.
wrong.No, a drop is never a pullback: A short, orderly drop onto a rising line fits if no day is over 2 ATR.
wrong.Yes, the 50-day has no length rule: The 2 to 8 session length applies on this card whichever line the stock touches.

questions.story: BFAM, 2019. A three-day drop onto the rising 50 SMA in a steady grinder. The dip is 2.24 ATR deep.
questions.simple: Yes, because the pullback rule is 2 to 8 sessions, and three sessions is inside that.

deeper.counter: Three days is enough, but the drop still has to be orderly, with no single down day larger than 2 ATR, and at least 1 ATR deep. BFAM was 2.24 ATR deep onto a rising 50 SMA.

reasons: the 2 to 8 session length is a proposed card number (map.length)

questions.q: What do you do with this one?
choices: Buy, it dipped and came back
Pass, it's slicing the line
Call it a Remount and wait
Buy, but with a wider stop
questions.why: Pass. In an 8-session pullback it closed under the line three times. That line isn't holding anything. A real pullback respects its line on the close. When a stock slices back and forth through it, there's no clean low to risk against. There's no sign buyers are defending it either. It hasn't sat under long enough to be a Remount. Nothing to buy, move on.
questions.lesson_line: A line sliced back and forth isn't a line held. Move on.

wrong.Call it a Remount and wait: A Remount loses the line for days on end. This just keeps chopping through it.
wrong.Buy, but with a wider stop: A wider stop doesn't fix a line that keeps getting sliced.
wrong.Buy, it dipped and came back: Coming back isn't the test. It kept closing under the line, so the line isn't support.

questions.story: The day before the would-be buy. In an 8-session pullback, the stock closed under the moving average it was testing three times.
questions.simple: Pass. It keeps closing under the line, so the line isn't support and there's no clean spot to risk against.

deeper.trap: Count closes, not hopes. Close after close under the line in one pullback is a line sliced, not held.

reasons: the two-close and five-close limits are proposed card numbers

questions.q: It took 10 sessions to get here. How do you handle it?

Skip it, the drift ran too long
Buy it now, before the trigger
Wait for a dip to the 50-day

On a rising 20 EMA a slower drift is normal, and that setup has its own plan. So name the line it's sitting on and run that plan: the trigger, the stop under the low, the size. Don't throw away a good name because it missed one setup.
questions.lesson_line: A slow drift isn't a bad stock. Judge it on the right setup.

wrong.Skip it, the drift ran too long: Ten quiet sessions onto a rising 20 EMA isn't a flaw. It's the slower version, so judge it there.
wrong.Buy it now, before the trigger: We buy as price trades through the trigger, never ahead of it.
wrong.Wait for a dip to the 50-day: It's sitting on its 20 EMA now. Judge the setup in front of you, not a deeper one you hope for.

questions.story: The day before the would-be buy. A leader drifted 10 sessions from its high onto its rising 20 EMA. Everything else looks right.
questions.simple: Judge it as a 20 EMA pullback. A slower drift onto a rising 20 EMA is normal, not a reason to skip.

deeper.trap: Missing one setup isn't a verdict on the stock. Ask which setup it fits before you throw it away.

The length of the dip
The 10-day line is rising
The volume on the dip days

questions.lesson_line: A stock far under its high is recovering, not leading.

wrong.The length of the dip: That check passes here. Exactly one check fails, and it is the distance from the high.
wrong.The 10-day line is rising: That check passes here. The distance from the 52-week high is what fails.
wrong.The volume on the dip days: Volume is not what fails here. Exactly one check fails, and it is the distance from the 52-week high.

questions.simple: The stock is 32.7 percent under its 52-week high, and a leader must be within 25 percent.

deeper.trap: Do not let a rising 10-day talk you in. The line can be right and the stock still fails the leader test. Here the close is 32.7% under the high, and the card allows 25%.

questions.q: How should that 4.5 times volume change your view?

Warning, it lowers the grade
Bullish, buyers stepped in
Nothing, volume is noise

There's a more basic problem anyway: it closed under the line, so there's no hold yet. Wait for a close back on the line before you think about a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy selling into the line lowers the grade. It doesn't void the setup.

wrong.It kills the setup, no trade: Heavy selling is a warning and a lower grade. It doesn't void the setup on its own.
wrong.Bullish, buyers stepped in: A close under the line on heavy volume is selling. It lowers the grade.

questions.simple: It's a distribution day. Be mindful and lower the grade, but it doesn't kill the setup.

deeper.trap: Heavy volume feels like a veto. It isn't. What still needs fixing is the close under the line, not the volume.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Move the stop down and wait it out
Buy again at once at the same price
Take it; re-enter on a new trigger
Drop the setup; the loss proves it fails
questions.answer: Take it; re-enter on a new trigger
questions.why: Take the loss, and buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. The loss does not mean the rule failed. The index was topping into a correction that same week, which the rule cannot see.
questions.lesson_line: A planned loss is the system working. Re-enter only on a new trigger.

wrong.Move the stop down and wait it out: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Buy again at once at the same price: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade.
wrong.Drop the setup; the loss proves it fails: One stop-out proves nothing about the rule. A planned loss is the system working, and the index was topping that week.

questions.story: NVDA, April 2024 (prices split-adjusted). A clean pullback with stacked, rising averages. You bought at 90.10 with the stop at 87.57. Next day the stop is hit.
questions.simple: Take the stop-out and re-enter only on a new trigger as a new trade, since one planned loss does not break the rule.

deeper.counter: After a stop-out the pull is to buy right back or to size up. Both break the rule. Wait for the setup to trigger again, then treat it as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. This loss came the day after the buy, with the index topping that week.

questions.q: You followed the plan and still lost. What's the takeaway?
choices: A normal cost of the setup
Should've waited one more day
The stop was too tight
Never buy the 50-day again
questions.answer: A normal cost of the setup
questions.why: A normal cost of the setup. Everything checked out, you bought the trigger, and the stop sat under the low. Then the line gave way. That's how this setup fails, and the stop did its job. It never got near 3R. In our test only about one in four reached 3R before the stop, so losses at the stop are part of it. Judge the process, not one outcome.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out with every rule followed is a normal cost.

wrong.Should've waited one more day: That's hindsight. On the day, everything checked out.
wrong.The stop was too tight: The stop sat where the chart said you were wrong. Taking it means the plan worked.
wrong.Never buy the 50-day again: The 50-day pullback is one of our trades. One loss doesn't change that.

questions.story: A 50-day pullback that checked out. You buy at 109.07 with the stop at 106.28. The stop hits on day 2, and the low breaks the 50-day that same day.
questions.simple: A normal cost. You followed every step and the line gave way, so the stop did its job.

deeper.trap: Don't judge a rule by one outcome. A stop-out doesn't prove the setup wrong, and a win doesn't prove it right. In our scan the edge was roughly a one-in-four chance of 3R, so stops come with it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (A4, the stop is the exit)

questions.q: How many tries do you get at the same name?
choices: 3 in a week and 6 in a month
2 in a week and 4 in a month
1 try, then drop the name
No cap if each one triggers
questions.answer: 3 in a week and 6 in a month
questions.why: 3 a week, 6 a month. Each one is a brand new trade, with its own trigger, its own stop and every rule. This one came back and ran without you. That stings. But on the day, the stop was hit, and that was the right exit. If it sets up again, take it again. The cap keeps you from revenge-trading one name into the ground.
questions.lesson_line: Same stock: 3 tries a week, 6 a month. Each one is a new trade.

wrong.2 in a week and 4 in a month: Too tight. The cap is 3 a week and 6 a month.
wrong.1 try, then drop the name: A stop-out doesn't end the name. A new trigger is a new trade, inside the cap.
wrong.No cap if each one triggers: There is a cap: 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock.

questions.story: You bought a pullback at 127.78 with the stop at 124.27. The stop hits on day 1, a one-day shakeout. The stock climbs later without you.
questions.simple: At most 3 tries a week and 6 a month on one stock, each one a new trade with its own trigger.

deeper.trap: Hindsight says it came back, so the shakeout looks like a gift. On the day, the stop was hit. The next buy needs its own trigger, its own stop and every rule again.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (settled) (B21 re-entry, E56 tries)

questions.q: What's the move?
choices: Get out now and take the loss
Wait for a bounce to the old stop
Move the stop to the day's low
Buy more to lower the average
questions.answer: Get out now and take the loss
questions.why: Get out. After a gap through your stop, the first 30 minutes decide, and that bar's low becomes your new stop. But if those 30 minutes already take the loss past 2R, you don't wait for anything. You're at 2.5R, so you're out. Hoping for a bounce to the old stop is how a planned loss turns into a disaster.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop: first 30 minutes decide. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Wait for a bounce to the old stop: The first 30 minutes decide, and past 2R you're out. Hoping isn't a plan.
wrong.Move the stop to the day's low: The 30-minute low is the new stop only when the loss isn't past 2R. You're past it.
wrong.Buy more to lower the average: Adding into a gap down is averaging down. One entry, one stop.

questions.story: You hold a pullback buy. It gaps down through your stop. After the first half hour you're down 2.5R on the trade.
questions.simple: Get out. The first 30 minutes already took the loss past 2R, and past 2R we're out.

deeper.trap: Two rules meet here. The new stop is the low of the first 30-minute bar. But if those 30 minutes already take the loss past 2R, you don't wait for a new stop. You get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 and the 2R exit)

questions.q: Pullback to buy, or something else?

A pullback, only 20.6% off the high
A pullback, first touches are best
A correction, any 3 ATR drop is one

That's a broken leader, not a leader resting. When a broken leader touches the 50-day for the first time, it's a correction. I'd leave it alone until it proves itself.

wrong.A pullback, only 20.6% off the high: 20.6% off the high doesn't make it a pullback. The flat 50-day says the trend stalled.
wrong.A pullback, first touches are best: First touches are best on a rising line in a working trend, not on a broken leader.
wrong.A correction, any 3 ATR drop is one: Depth alone isn't the test. The flat line and the broken trend are.

questions.story: The day before the trigger. A former leader is 20.6% off its high, with a flat 50 SMA. It fell 3.6 ATR and touches the 50-day for the first time.
questions.simple: A correction. The 50-day is flat and the stock fell hard, so it's a broken leader, not a pullback.

deeper.trap: It's easy to stop at 20.6% off the high and call it fine. The 50 SMA was flat, the 200 was rising into it and the dip was 3.6 ATR deep. That's a correction.

Size down a lot, or skip
Move the stop up to 3%

Sell it, free the money
Sell half, trail the rest
Wait for 3R, then decide

questions.lesson_line: Ten trading days under 1R, and the money moves on.

wrong.Sell half, trail the rest: The time stop sells the whole trade, not half.

Take it, it's sitting on the line
Pass, the average is rolling over
Pass, the dip is too shallow

A clean read isn't a promise, though.

wrong.Take it, it's sitting on the line: Being on the line isn't the reason. The calm dip and the hold are.
wrong.Pass, the average is rolling over: Look again. The line is rising, and the stock has ridden it for months.
wrong.Pass, the dip is too shallow: 1.42 ATR is a real rest for this stock. Shallow and quiet is fine.

Pass, it's way under its high
Pass, the dip is too short
Take it, volume fell on the dip

The rising line and the touch look nice, but the first question is whether it's a leader at all. A bounce out of a hole that deep is a different trade.

questions.q: What do you tell him?

He's right, most pullbacks win
Skip it, 27.7% is too low
Size up, the test proves our edge
questions.answer: No, size comes from the stop

questions.lesson_line: Never size up on a win-rate claim. Size comes from the stop.

wrong.He's right, most pullbacks win: The test says otherwise. About one in four reached 3R before the stop.

wrong.Size up, the test proves our edge: The test used a fixed stop with no sells, so it can't prove our exact edge. Size still comes from the stop.

questions.story: A friend says this setup wins most of the time, so you should size up. Our test of 60,464 pullbacks found 27.7% reached 3R before the stop.
questions.simple: Size comes from the stop and the risk rules. Only about one in four reached 3R, so a win-rate claim changes nothing.

deeper.counter: Both easy reads are wrong. Most pullbacks don't win: only 27.7% reached 3R before the stop. But 27.7% isn't a reason to skip either, since the test used a fixed stop with no sells. The edge is the one-in-four shot at 3R and one-in-six at 5R.

Sell now, it broke the 9 EMA
Hold, but switch to the 20 EMA
Add back the shares you sold

questions.q: The stock blew through your level. What went wrong?
choices: No stop order with the broker
The stop wasn't tight enough
No price alert set at 30.67
The size was too big
questions.answer: No stop order with the broker
questions.why: No stop order with the broker. Every position gets one the moment you're in. A stop in your head only works when you're watching, and you won't always be watching. A price alert just tells you, it doesn't sell. With the order in, it sells near 30.67 while you're on that call. Instead you're looking at 29.90.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an order with the broker, not a number in your head.

wrong.The stop wasn't tight enough: Distance wasn't the problem. Nothing was there to sell at 30.67.
wrong.No price alert set at 30.67: An alert only tells you. It doesn't sell. The stop has to be an order.
wrong.The size was too big: The size came from the stop, so size wasn't what failed. Nothing was there to sell at 30.67.

questions.story: You buy a pullback at 31.80 and plan to sell if it trades under 30.67. At 2 pm you're on a call, and the stock trades 29.90.
questions.simple: There was no stop order with the broker. A plan in your head can't sell when you're away.

deeper.trap: An alert feels like protection, but it only tells you. On a call at 2 pm you'd see it late, with the price already through. Only an order with the broker acts without you.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, a live stop order with the broker)

questions.q: A pullback needs more room, so you move the stop lower to keep the trade alive.
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up. If the stock is hitting your stop, the trade isn't working. That's the information. Lowering it just turns a small planned loss into a bigger one. If it needs a wider stop, decide that before the buy and size for it. The one exception is a gap through the stop, and that has its own rule.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only moves up. Never lower it to keep a trade alive.
questions.simple: False. The stop only moves up, and lowering it turns a planned loss into a bigger one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop only moves up)

Right after the fill, at the entry
As soon as the trade is up 1R
Once the last third starts to trail

questions.why: When the first third comes off. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. The first trim is a third at 3R, so the default lands at 3R, inside that window.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, by default at the first trim.

wrong.Right after the fill, at the entry: That is not the rule. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R.
wrong.As soon as the trade is up 1R: 1R is under the window. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R.
wrong.Once the last third starts to trail: That is after the 5R trim. The default is the first trim.

questions.lesson_line: Know your 2R the day you buy. The breakeven window opens there.

questions.q: What's your move into this?
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Add at the gap, it's strong
Hold it all, trail the 20 EMA
Sell a fixed third, like always
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Gap after gap on rising volume and the widest bar of the move: that's a climax run. A burst like this can mark the end of the leg for a while. Sell a big part into the strength while buyers are paying up. How much is your call. Never add here. You'd be buying right where you should be selling.
questions.lesson_line: Into a climax run, sell a big part. How much is your call.

wrong.Add at the gap, it's strong: Never into a climax. That's where we sell, not where we buy more.
wrong.Hold it all, trail the 20 EMA: On a climax run we sell a big part into it. We don't wait for the trail.
wrong.Sell a fixed third, like always: There's no fixed third. On a climax run you sell a big part, and how much is your call.

questions.story: Your pullback buy has run four days and is still short of 3R. It gapped up twice on rising volume, and today it gaps up again on its widest range yet.

deeper.trap: Selling a big part isn't selling everything, and how much is your call. Adding into a climax because the run looks strong is the opposite. Never add into a burst like this.

questions.q: You'll see ATR on every pullback we study. What does it actually measure?
choices: How volatile the stock has been
Which way the trend points
How heavy the volume has been
How far it sits from its high
questions.answer: How volatile the stock has been
questions.why: How volatile the stock has been. ATR, the average true range, is the size of a normal day's move, gaps included. It doesn't tell you direction. We use it to judge a dip against the stock's own range. A small dip on a wild stock is just noise. The same dip on a quiet stock is a real move.
questions.lesson_line: ATR is the stock's normal daily range. Judge dips against it.
questions.simple: ATR measures how much the stock moves on a normal day, gaps included. It doesn't tell you direction.

wrong.Which way the trend points: ATR has no direction. It only measures how much the stock moves.
wrong.How heavy the volume has been: ATR measures price movement, not volume.
wrong.How far it sits from its high: That's distance off the high. ATR is a stock's normal daily range.

reasons: fills the gap that ATR is used in every depth, touch and orderly rule but was never defined

questions.story: You bought a pullback on Monday. Your 5R level is 42.50. News hits overnight, and on Thursday, day 4, the stock opens at 43.10.
questions.q: It opens over your 5R level. How do you handle the open?
choices: Weigh selling some into the gap
Sell a third, 5R is the rule
Sell everything left at the open
Add, it just gapped up
questions.answer: Weigh selling some into the gap
questions.why: Weigh selling some into the gap. It opened at 43.10, over your 5R level of 42.50, on day 4 of the push. A gap past a profit level isn't an automatic sell. But day 4 of a strong push, on news, is a fair spot for a first sell. Selling part here is your judgment. Holding the rest on the trail is fine too. Adding into the gap isn't the plan.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over a profit level is a time to weigh a sale, not a rule.

wrong.Sell everything left at the open: We sell in parts and trail the rest. A gap up isn't an exit signal.
wrong.Sell a third, 5R is the rule: No profit level is a rule. The first sell is a judgment, and a gap doesn't force it.
wrong.Add, it just gapped up: A gap isn't a reason to add. An add to a winner is rare, a feel call, never the plan.

questions.simple: Weigh selling some. A gap past a profit level never forces a sale, and day 4 is a fair spot for a first sell.

deeper.trap: A gap past a profit level feels like an order to sell. It isn't. Selling part at the open is one choice you may make, and holding the rest on the trail is another.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, take the trim at the open; E51, a third at 5R)
